draft.title: Vector proofs
card: To prove a geometry result, write the sides as vectors. Name two sides from one corner, such as a and b, then write every other side or diagonal using a and b.
Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is 0. So to prove two lines are perpendicular, show that the scalar product of their vectors is 0.
Worked example: a rhombus OABC has OA = a and OC = b, with |a| = |b| because all sides are equal. The diagonals are OB = a + b and AC = b − a.
Then (a + b)·(b − a) = b·b − a·a = |b|² − |a|² = 0. So the diagonals are perpendicular.
draft.remember: Write the shape in terms of a and b, then show the scalar product is 0.

a.q: To prove that two diagonals of a shape are perpendicular, what must you show about their vectors?
opts: Their vector sum is the zero vector
a.why: Non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their scalar product is 0. Equal magnitudes do not make lines perpendicular: the diagonals of a rectangle are equal in length but are not usually perpendicular.
a.clue: Think of the test for perpendicular vectors.

b.q: In a rhombus, OA = a, OC = b and |a| = |b|. Which step gives (a + b)·(b − a) = 0?
opts: It expands to |b|² − |a|², and the sides are equal
It expands to |a|² − |b|², and the sides are equal
It expands to |a|² + |b|², and the sides are equal
It expands to a·b − a·b, and the sides are parallel
b.why: Expanding gives a·b − a·a + b·b − b·a. The a·b terms cancel, leaving |b|² − |a|². Equal side lengths make this 0. The option with a plus sign is wrong because the a·a term is subtracted, not added.
b.clue: The two a·b terms cancel, so check which squares are left and their signs.

b.best: It expands to |b|² − |a|², and the sides are equal
